overview: Iceland is an island country in the North Atlantic, just south of the Arctic Circle. Its capital, Reykjavík, is the northernmost capital of any independent country. Iceland was settled by Norse people in the 800s, and its parliament, the Althing, founded in 930, is one of the oldest in the world. It became fully independent from Denmark in 1944.

geography.text: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two tectonic plates are pulling apart, which is why it has so many volcanoes, hot springs and geysers. Glaciers cover about a tenth of the land, including Vatnajökull, one of the largest in Europe. Most people live along the coast, while the interior is a high plateau of lava fields and ice where almost nobody lives.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Cool summers and mild winters for its latitude, thanks to the Gulf Stream, but windy and changeable.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Millions of puffins nest on the cliffs, and whales feed in the seas around the island.

history.text: Norse settlers arrived in Iceland from the late 800s, and in 930 they founded the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments. Iceland later came under Norwegian and then Danish rule. It became a sovereign kingdom linked to Denmark in 1918 and a fully independent republic in 1944.

events.title: First settlers
events.text: By tradition, Ingólfur Arnarson settles at Reykjavík.

events.title: Norwegian rule
events.text: Iceland accepts the rule of the Norwegian king.

events.title: Republic
events.text: Iceland becomes a fully independent republic.

events.title: First elected woman president
events.text: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir becomes the world's first democratically elected female president.

government.text: Iceland is a parliamentary republic. Its parliament, the Althing, first met in 930 and is one of the oldest in the world. It chooses the Prime Minister, while the President is elected directly every four years. Iceland is a founding member of NATO but has no army, and it is not in the European Union.

economy.text: Fishing was long the base of Iceland's economy and is still a big export. Tourism has grown enormously, drawn by glaciers, volcanoes and the northern lights. Cheap geothermal and hydro power attracts aluminium smelters and data centres. Iceland's banks collapsed in the 2008 financial crisis, and the country recovered quickly afterwards.

culture.text: Icelanders can still read the medieval sagas written in Old Norse, because their language has changed so little. Most Icelanders have no family surname: their last name comes from their father's or mother's first name, such as Jónsdóttir, 'Jón's daughter'. Iceland also has one of the highest numbers of published writers per person in the world.

items.title: The sagas
items.text: Stories of Viking-age families, written down in the 1200s.

items.title: Geothermal pools
items.text: Hot springs heat most homes and fill outdoor swimming pools.

items.title: Björk
items.text: The singer is Iceland's best-known musician.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Lamb, fish and skyr, a thick yoghurt-like cheese. Fermented shark, hákarl, is a famous challenge for visitors.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: The medieval sagas are Iceland's great literary treasure, and modern bands such as Sigur Rós are famous abroad.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: Thirteen mischievous Yule Lads visit children in the days before Christmas, leaving gifts or a potato in shoes left on windowsills.

sport.text: Handball is Iceland's national sport, and its men won Olympic silver in 2008. In football, Iceland became the smallest country ever to reach a World Cup, in 2018, two years after beating England at Euro 2016. Its fans' 'thunderclap' chant became famous.

items.title: Euro 2016
items.text: Iceland beat England 2–1 to reach the quarter-finals.
The smallest country by population to play at a men's World Cup.

items.title: Strongmen
items.text: Icelanders have won World's Strongest Man many times.

didYouKnow: Iceland has no army; it is defended through NATO.
About two-thirds of Iceland's people live in and around Reykjavík.

keyPeople.name: Björk
keyPeople.text: Known for experimental pop music and striking music videos.

keyPeople.name: Leif Erikson
keyPeople.text: Born in Iceland around 970; reached North America around 1000.

keyPeople.name: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir
keyPeople.text: The world's first democratically elected female president, in 1980.
